title: Why Open Minds Can Still Split Into Two Camps
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Opinion Dynamics and Bounded Confidence: Models, Analysis, and Simulation
source.venue: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation (JASSS), vol. 5, no. 3

intro.summary: The paper asks when a group of people who keep adjusting their opinions to each other ends in agreement, in two opposed camps, or in many scattered views. It reviews older 'averaging' models, in which repeated averaging tends toward consensus. It then studies a model where each person only listens to others whose opinions are close enough to their own: their 'bounded confidence'. Proofs and computer simulations show that as this listening range grows, the group moves from many opinions, to two camps, to one consensus. They also find that a bias toward one's own side pushes the camps out to the extremes. The main limitation is that these are idealised mathematical models with one-dimensional opinions and everyone able to hear everyone. They are not tested against data from real people.
background: An opinion here is just a number between 0 and 1, like a position on a left–right scale or an estimate of some quantity.
'Averaging' means a person replaces their view with a weighted mix of the views they pay attention to.
A simulation runs a rule many times on a computer to see what pattern it produces. It is useful when the equations are too hard to solve by hand.
A model can show that a mechanism is able to produce an outcome. It cannot show that real societies actually work that way.
intro.aha: People who listen to a fairly wide range of views, but not to everyone, typically do not meet in the middle. They split into two lasting camps, because the edges bunch up and pull the centre apart.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Groups of people talk, listen and update their views. Sometimes they converge on one view, sometimes they split into two hostile camps, and sometimes many separate opinions survive. The authors want to know which simple rules of listening lead to which of these outcomes.
primer.quote: When does opinion formation within an interacting group lead to consensus, polarization or fragmentation?

primer.heading: The old answer: averaging brings agreement
primer.body: Earlier models, from French in 1956 to DeGroot and Lehrer in the 1970s, assume each person takes a weighted average of others' opinions, round after round. If the listening links are connected enough, these models predict consensus almost every time. That made it hard for them to explain why real communities split.
primer.quote: Since universal ultimate agreement is an ubiquitous outcome of a very broad class of mathematical models, we are naturally led to inquire what on earth one must assume in order to generate the bimodal outcome of community cleavage studies.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: They add one realistic twist: people only take seriously those whose opinions lie within a certain distance of their own, the 'confidence level'. Because who you listen to now depends on what everyone thinks, the model becomes nonlinear and hard to solve with formulas. So alongside a few proofs, they ran many computer simulations with 625 randomly placed opinions, slowly widening the confidence level.
primer.quote: For that reason we carry out the analysis of the above nonlinear model to a large extent by simulations on the computer.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: With a tiny listening range many small clusters survive. With a middle-sized range the group typically ends in two camps, one on each side. With a wide range everyone meets in the middle. The two camps form because people at the edges are pulled only inward, so they bunch up. These bunches then pull in nearby people, and the profile cracks in the middle. Once cracked, the pieces never reconnect. When people listen more to their own side, the camps end up even further apart.
primer.quote: As the homogeneous and symmetric confidence interval increases we transit from phase to phase. More exactly, we step from fragmentation (plurality) over polarisation (polarity) to consensus (conformity).

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: The model shows that polarisation does not need extremists or hostility. Fairly open-minded people who simply average nearby views can split into two camps. These are stylised models, not measurements: opinions are a single number, everyone can in principle hear everyone, and the numbers come from simulations rather than surveys. The authors note that restricting talk to local neighbourhoods changed the picture sharply in early tests.
primer.quote: At least under bounded confidence locality of interactions may prevent societies from sharp polarisation.

concepts.title: Averaging again and again pulls opinions together
concepts.idea: If each person repeatedly replaces their opinion with a weighted average that includes the other's opinion, the gap between them shrinks every round until they agree.

predict.question: A new case: Ben is completely stubborn and never listens. Ann gives Ben a 20% say every round. Ann starts at 0.2 and Ben at 0.8. Where do they end up?
options: They never agree, because Ben won't budge
They agree at Ben's opinion, 0.8
They agree halfway, at 0.5
Ann overshoots and ends above 0.8
why: It feels as if both people must move to agree. But the gap is multiplied by 1 − 0.2 − 0 = 0.8 every round, so it still shrinks to zero. Only Ann does the moving.
Correct. Ben's opinion never changes. Ann keeps taking 20% of the remaining distance to him, so the gap shrinks every round and she settles on his 0.8.
Halfway is where they meet when both listen equally. Here only Ann listens, so the meeting point is pulled all the way to Ben.
Each new opinion of Ann's is a mix of her old one and Ben's, so it always lies between the two. A mix can never land outside them.

terms.means: A mix of opinions where each one counts by a set share, and the shares add up to 1
The share one person gives to someone's opinion when forming their own new opinion
Everyone ending up with the same opinion

model.title: Two opinions, round after round
model.note: Teaching model: just two people, opinions on a 0–1 scale, listening shares that never change, and lines drawn smoothly between whole rounds. Starting opinions 0.2 and 0.8 are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: How much Ann listens to Ben
How much Ben listens to Ann

outputs.label: Share of the gap kept each round

steps.say: Two people, Ann and Ben, hold opinions on a scale from 0 to 1. Time runs left to right, one round of talking at a time.
The blue line is Ann. She starts at 0.2. The orange line is Ben. He starts at 0.8.
This slider sets how much Ann listens to Ben each round. Watch her line bend.
This one sets how much Ben listens to Ann.
This slider picks a round to read off. The boxes show the gap between them, and each person's opinion, at that round.

explore.prompt: Play with how much each person listens. How fast can you close the gap, and can you choose where they meet?

goals.text: Make Ann and Ben agree, with a gap under 0.01, by round 5 or earlier
hints: Which sliders make the gap shrink faster each round?
Watch the 'share of the gap kept each round' box. You want it small, so both people need to listen more.
Raise both listening sliders together and stop when the gap at round 5 is under 0.01.

goals.text: Make them agree (gap under 0.02) at an opinion above 0.7, much nearer Ben's start
hints: For the meeting point to land near Ben, who has to do most of the moving?
Make Ann listen a lot and Ben listen only a little. Then read off a late round.
Push Ann's listening to the top, Ben's almost to the bottom, and read off the last round.

feedback.correct: Right. Only one person needs to keep listening. The gap is still multiplied by a number below 1 every round, so it vanishes. The stubborn person's opinion is where they meet.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed both people must move, or that they always meet halfway. Each round Ann's new opinion is a mix of hers and Ben's. So she closes a fixed share of the remaining distance and lands on Ben's unchanging 0.8.

steps.say: Start with nobody listening. Each keeps their own opinion every round. The lines stay flat and the gap stays at 0.6 forever.
Now Ann gives Ben a 10% say. Each round her new opinion is 90% her old one plus 10% of Ben's. That mix is a weighted average, and the 10% is the weight she gives Ben.
Let Ben do the same, with a weight of 10% on Ann. Now both lines bend toward each other.
Each round the gap keeps 1 − 0.1 − 0.1 = 80% of its size. So 0.6 becomes 0.48, then about 0.38. It shrinks by the same fraction every round and never grows back.
Run it longer. By round 20 the gap is almost nothing. When everyone ends up holding the same opinion, we call it consensus.
Listen more and the shrinking speeds up. With weights of 0.3 each, every round keeps only 40% of the gap. Look how small it already is by round 5.
The weights also decide where they meet. Ann now listens a lot and Ben only a little. Ann does most of the moving, and they meet at 0.68, much nearer Ben's start.

understand.explanation: Each round, each person replaces their opinion with a weighted average of their own opinion and the other's. Both move toward each other, so the gap is multiplied by the same fraction every round: 1 minus the two weights. It therefore shrinks again and again toward zero. Bigger weights close it faster, and the person who listens more moves further. If both weights are zero, nothing ever changes. The paper calls this the classical model (from DeGroot and Lehrer). Its Result 1 states a precise condition: consensus is approached from any starting opinions if, for any two people, there is some third person (who may be one of them) on whom both put positive weight. This is a mathematical result about a model with fixed weights, not an observation of real groups.
understand.quote: Intuitively, one may expect that this process of repeatedly averaging opinions will bring newly formed opinions of different agents closer to each other until they flow into a consensus among all agents.

connect.caption: The first part is the paper's equation (2.1) written for two people. Person 1 is Ann and person 2 is Ben. a_{12} is how much Ann listens to Ben (the blue slider). Her own share a_{11} is what is left, 1 − a_{12}, because the weights add up to 1. Ben's rule is the same, with a_{21} (the orange slider). Subtracting the two rules gives this model's gap rule: each round the gap is multiplied by 1 − a_{12} − a_{21}, which is the 'share kept each round' box.

concepts.recap: Repeatedly mixing your opinion with someone else's shrinks the gap by the same fraction every round, so as long as someone keeps listening, the two end up agreeing. If no one listens, nothing changes.

concepts.title: Only listening to people who are close
concepts.idea: Under bounded confidence a person averages only the opinions within a distance ε of their own and ignores everyone further away.

predict.question: Cara holds opinion 0.50 and listens to anyone within 0.20 of her. Dan holds 0.65 and Eve holds 0.95. Using the paper's rule, where is Cara's opinion after one round?
options: About 0.58
About 0.70
She stays at 0.50
Exactly 0.65
why: Correct: Dan is 0.15 away, inside her range. Eve is 0.45 away, outside it. Cara averages herself and Dan with equal weight: (0.50 + 0.65) ÷ 2 = 0.575.
Tempting if you average all three people, as in plain averaging. Eve is beyond 0.20 from Cara, so under this rule she counts for nothing.
Tempting if you think one disagreeing voice is not enough to move her. Dan is inside the range, so he gets a full equal share of her average.
Tempting if you think she simply adopts the view of whoever she listens to. She averages, and her own opinion is part of that average, so she lands halfway.

terms.means: How far from your own opinion you are willing to listen. Opinions further away than ε are ignored completely.
The rule that each person averages only the opinions within ε of their own, giving each of them equal weight.

model.title: Who you listen to, and where your opinion lands next
model.note: Teaching model: only you update while five other people stay frozen in place. In the paper everyone updates at the same time. As in the paper, everyone inside the band gets equal weight, and you count yourself. The opinion positions are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: This line runs from opinion 0 on the left to opinion 1 on the right. Each dot is one person's opinion on some question.
The dot labelled You is your opinion. This slider slides it along the line.
The shaded band shows how far you are willing to listen. This slider makes the band wider or narrower.
People inside the band light up. A line runs from each of them to the point marked Next round.
That point is where your opinion sits after one round of thinking it over. Its exact value is shown here.

explore.prompt: Play with your position and your listening band. See how the crowd inside the band decides where you go.

goals.text: Get exactly two other people into your listening band, so three opinions go into your average.
hints: Right now only one other person is inside the band. What would let more people in?
Widen the band with the listening distance slider, and watch the count of people in your average.
With your opinion at 0.50, set the listening distance to 0.20. The people at 0.44 and 0.33 are in, and 0.71 is just outside.

goals.text: Make your opinion move to the right (upward) next round.
hints: You move toward the average of the people in your band. When would that average sit to your right?
Slide your own opinion so the nearest person inside the band is to your right, and the people to your left drop out.
Keep the band at 0.10 and move your opinion to about 0.65. Then only the person at 0.71 is inside.

feedback.correct: Right. Dan is within 0.20 of Cara and Eve is not. Cara averages only herself and Dan, with equal weights, and lands at about 0.58. Eve has no effect at all, however extreme she is.
feedback.incorrect: The key is the window. First check who is within 0.20 of Cara: Dan at 0.65 is, Eve at 0.95 is not. Then take a plain equal-weight average of Cara and the people inside the window. Eve counts for nothing, and Cara does not simply copy Dan.

steps.say: Start with the band shrunk to nothing. You hear no one, so your average is just yourself. You stay put at 0.50.
Widen the band to 0.10. One person, at 0.44, is now inside. You average with them and land at about 0.47. The paper calls this listening distance the confidence level ε.
At ε = 0.20 the person at 0.33 joins too. Three opinions, equal weight each: (0.50 + 0.44 + 0.33) ÷ 3 ≈ 0.42.
Now look at the person at 0.71. They are only 0.21 away, just outside the band. They do not count a little less. They count not at all.
Nudge ε to 0.25 and they cross inside. Your next opinion jumps from about 0.42 to about 0.50. One person entering the window changes the whole average.
At ε = 0.40 everyone is inside, and you are back to plain averaging with the whole group, as in the last lesson. Averaging only inside the window is called bounded confidence.
Now set ε to 0.20 and move yourself to 0.65. A different crowd is in your band, just the person at 0.71, so you drift right. Who you listen to depends on where you stand.

understand.explanation: Under bounded confidence you still average opinions, but only those within your confidence level ε of your own. Everyone inside the window gets an equal share. Everyone outside gets nothing, even if they are only slightly beyond the edge. So who counts is decided by the current opinions themselves, and the weights change as opinions move. This is what makes the model nonlinear. The authors note that standard matrix tools no longer apply and that clear-cut maths results are hard to get. That is why they mostly studied the model with computer simulations, for example with 625 randomly placed opinions. The model is a deliberate simplification: in their main analysis everyone uses the same ε and weights everyone in range equally.
understand.quote: An agent i takes only those agents j into account whose opinions differ from his own not more than a certain confidence level

connect.caption: This is the paper's bounded-confidence model (BC) with the set (2.3). Your opinion x_{i} is the You slider. ε is the listening distance. I(i, x) is the set of people inside the band, and |I| is how many there are, you included. Your next opinion x_{i}(t+1) is a plain average over that set.

concepts.recap: Under bounded confidence you average only the opinions within ε of your own, with equal weight. Anyone further away is ignored, so who you listen to shifts as opinions move.

concepts.title: Many opinions, two camps, or one
concepts.idea: When the confidence range is widened, a whole population passes from many surviving opinions, to two camps, to a single consensus.

predict.question: Keep the listening range at 0.15, which on a full 0-to-1 line often gives two camps. Now everyone starts bunched in the middle half, between 0.25 and 0.75, instead of spread over the whole line. What end result is most likely?
options: Still two camps, exactly as on the full line
More groups, because the crowd is packed tighter
One group, or very close to it
Nobody moves, because the range is too small
why: Tempting if you think the range alone fixes the outcome. What matters is how wide the range is compared with how spread out the opinions are.
Packing people closer puts more of them within reach of each other. That is the opposite of splitting into more groups.
Correct. The opinions now cover only half the line, so 0.15 acts like a range of about 0.3 on the full line. That is in the one-group region.
With opinions packed this tight, almost everyone has many people within 0.15, so averaging starts at once.

terms.means: Many separate opinion groups survive at the end and never merge
The population ends up in two separated camps
A stretch of settings where the end result looks alike, the way ice and water are phases of one substance

model.title: A crowd of 100 people settling their opinions
model.note: Teaching model: 100 people hold opinions from 0 to 1. Each round, everyone at once moves to the average of all opinions within the listening range: the paper's own rule. Groups are counted by gaps wider than 0.1, so tiny stray groups at the edges also count. Ranges below 0.06 are left out because nearby groups there would be merged in the count. The paper used 625 people, so its switch points differ a little. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Listening range (how far away an opinion can be and still be heard)

outputs.label: Distance between the two most extreme opinions
Share of the opinion line one person can hear

steps.say: Each dot is one person. Their opinion is a number from 0 to 1. Everyone starts scattered at random.
This slider is the listening range. Each person only listens to opinions closer to their own than this.
When the talking stops, this box counts how many separate groups are left.
This box shows how far apart the two most extreme people still are.
And this slider deals out a fresh random crowd, so you can check that a result is not just luck.

explore.prompt: Slide the listening range from wide to narrow and watch how the crowd ends up. Then try a few different starting crowds.

goals.text: With a narrow range (0.12 or less), break the crowd into at least 4 separate groups
hints: Should people hear more or fewer others for the crowd to stay split up?
Move the listening range toward its narrow end.
Keep narrowing below where camps form, and watch the group count climb.

goals.text: With a middle-sized range (0.24 or less), get the crowd to end in two or three camps
hints: The camps live between 'many groups' and 'one group'.
Start from about 0.24 and narrow the range slowly, watching the group count.
Camps form in a band just below where the whole crowd joins up. Stop when the count reads 2 or 3.

feedback.correct: Yes. What sets the end result is how wide the listening range is compared with how spread out opinions are. Halve the spread and the same range acts twice as wide, which pushes the crowd toward one group.
feedback.incorrect: The range is not a fixed recipe for two camps. Its effect depends on how far apart people start. If opinions are packed into half the line, 0.15 covers as large a share of the crowd as 0.3 would on the full line, which is consensus territory.

steps.say: Start wide. Each person can hear opinions up to 0.5 away. Watch nearly everyone slide together into one big group.

Narrow to 0.30. Each person now hears only part of the line, yet most of the crowd still ends up together. Chains of nearby listeners link people up. A tiny stray group at an edge can add to the count.
Now 0.20. The big group breaks apart, and camps form on either side of the middle. The spread now measures the gap between them. This two-camp outcome is called polarisation.
Narrower still, 0.12. Instead of two camps, several groups survive.
At 0.06, people hear only near neighbours. Many small groups survive side by side. Many opinions surviving is called plurality.
Is this luck? Deal a different random crowd. The group count stays in the same ballpark. The range, not the starting crowd, sets the type of outcome.
So three regions appear: many groups, then a few camps, then one. Each region is called a phase. Here is the puzzling middle one: separate camps, even though people are fairly open-minded.

understand.explanation: Each person only averages with opinions within their listening range, ε. When ε is tiny, people form small local clusters that never meet, so many opinions survive. At middle values the crowd ends in two camps. Once ε is large enough, chains of listeners link everyone and one consensus forms. The paper showed this by simulation, not proof. It placed 625 opinions at random, walked ε from 0.01 to 0.4 in 40 steps and repeated each step 50 times. In its single runs, ε = 0.01 left 38 opinions, ε = 0.15 gave two camps and ε = 0.25 gave consensus. Above 0.4 the result was always consensus. These switch points belong to the paper's own model and setup, so other rules or crowd sizes shift them.
understand.quote: As the homogeneous and symmetric confidence interval increases we transit from phase to phase. More exactly, we step from fragmentation (plurality) over polarisation (polarity) to consensus (conformity).

check.question: In the paper's runs, a listening range of ε = 0.25 already led to consensus, even though each person heard only half of the opinion line. Why can people who never hear the extremes still end up agreeing with them?

options.text: Chains of overlapping listeners link everyone, so averaging spreads step by step across the whole crowd
options.why: Right. Each person hears their neighbours, who hear theirs, and so on. Repeated averaging along these chains pulls the whole crowd together.

options.text: Consensus only happens when each person can hear the whole line, so the paper's result must be a fluke
options.why: The paper repeated each setting 50 times, and consensus at this range was typical, not a one-off run.

options.text: Wider ranges make people copy the most popular opinion directly
options.why: Nobody copies anyone. Each person takes a plain average of the opinions within range, and agreement builds up over many rounds.

check.hint: Think back to the walkthrough at 0.30. Nobody heard everyone, yet most people still ended together.
check.misconception: That consensus needs everyone to hear everyone. In fact, people who each hear only part of the line can be linked into one group through chains of nearby listeners.

connect.caption: The paper's bounded-confidence rule (BC). Each person i takes the plain average of everyone whose opinion is within ε of their own, and the model runs exactly this rule. The highlighted ε is the listening range slider. Widening it moves the crowd through the phases that the group count shows.

concepts.recap: Widen how far people listen, and a crowd moves from many surviving opinions, to two camps, to one consensus.

concepts.title: The edges are only pulled inward
concepts.idea: People near the extremes have neighbours on one side only, so averaging moves them toward the centre, while people in the middle are pulled equally both ways and barely move at first.

predict.question: New case: everyone's opinion starts evenly spread, but only between 0.2 and 0.8. Nobody holds an opinion below 0.2 or above 0.8. Everyone listens within the same range ε = 0.1. In the first round, who moves?
options: People near 0 and 1, the ends of the scale
People near 0.2 and 0.8, each pulled toward the centre
People near 0.5, because the centre attracts everyone
Everyone moves by the same amount
why: Tempting if you tie 'edge' to the ends of the scale. But nobody holds an opinion there, so nobody can move there. What matters is where the crowd ends.

Correct. Someone at 0.2 hears only people above them, and someone at 0.8 hears only people below. Their averages lean inward. People in the interior still hear a balanced window and stay put at first.
The centre does not pull on anyone directly. A person at 0.5 hears as many people above as below, so in the first round they do not move at all.
Averaging moves you only when your window is lopsided. Inside the crowd the window is balanced, so most people do not move in the first round.

terms.means: The situation of someone near an extreme: everyone within their listening range sits on one side of them, so averaging can only pull them one way
A starting set of opinions spaced evenly, with the same gap between each neighbouring pair

model.title: How far each opinion moves in the first round of averaging
model.note: Teaching model: opinions start as a smooth, perfectly even spread from 0 to 1 (like very many evenly spaced people). Each person replaces their opinion with the average of everyone within ε of it. The curve shows only the first round. Later rounds are not shown, because the spread stops being even once the edges move. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

outputs.label: Average of the opinions you hear
Share of people who move at all

y.label: Move in the first round (+ up, − down)

series.label: Move after one round of averaging
series.expr: (max(0, x - eps) + min(1, x + eps)) / 2 - x

steps.say: Picture a crowd whose opinions are spread evenly from 0 to 1. This curve shows how far each opinion moves after everyone averages once.
Above the flat line means pushed up. Below means pushed down. On the line means no move.
This slider places one opinion, yours. The dot shows how far it moves.
This slider sets ε, how far each person listens. The two lines mark ε in from each end of the scale.
Watch the curve change shape as the range changes.

explore.prompt: Move your opinion around the scale and stretch the listening range. Find where averaging pushes hardest, and where it does nothing at all.

goals.text: Find an opinion that gets pushed upward by more than 0.05 in the first round
hints: Upward pushes happen only where the crowd sits entirely on one side of you.
Slide your opinion close to 0, the bottom of the scale.
Go almost all the way to 0, closer to the edge than the listening range ε.

goals.text: Put your opinion at exactly 0.3, then make it start moving (by more than 0.01)
hints: At 0.3 with the default range, your window is balanced. Something must make it lopsided.
Your window becomes lopsided once it reaches past 0. Which slider makes the window wider?
Raise ε until it reaches past 0.3, so the bottom edge falls inside your reach.

feedback.correct: Right. The push comes from where the crowd ends, not from the numbers on the scale. People at the boundary of the occupied range hear only one side and drift inward. Everyone deeper inside hears a balanced window.
feedback.incorrect: The key is lopsidedness. Averaging moves you only if more of the people you hear sit on one side of you. That happens at the edges of the crowd, wherever those are. It does not happen at the scale's ends if no one is there, or in the middle.

steps.say: Start in the middle. An opinion at 0.5 with ε = 0.15 hears everyone from 0.35 to 0.65. As many people sit above it as below, so the average it hears is 0.5. It does not move.
Slide to 0.3. The window, 0.15 to 0.45, is still fully inside the scale and still balanced. The dot stays on the flat line.
Now try 0.1. Its window would reach down to −0.05, but nobody holds an opinion below 0. The people it hears sit mostly above it, so their average is 0.125. It moves up by 0.025.
At the very bottom, 0, everyone it hears is above it. This is one-sided influence: it can only be pulled one way. Here the pull is strongest, half of ε.
The top edge is the mirror image. An opinion at 0.95 hears only people below it, so it is pushed down.
Widen the range to 0.3. The edge zones grow, so more people feel a lopsided pull, and the pull is stronger. The centre still sits still.

This is only round one. The paper started from a regular start profile: evenly spaced opinions like these. Once the edges move in, their neighbours face a lopsided crowd too, so movement spreads toward the centre.

understand.explanation: When opinions are evenly spread, someone in the middle hears as many people above as below, so their average equals their own opinion and they stay put. Someone within ε of an end has nobody beyond that end to listen to. Everyone they hear sits on the inner side, so averaging pulls them toward the centre, hardest at the very edge. Hegselmann and Krause showed this by starting simulations from evenly spaced opinions (50, and later 500, with ε = 0.2). They then tracked how much each opinion changed per round. Change began at the extremes and spread inward with a delay, and the centre opinions were the last to be affected. This model shows only the first round and treats the crowd as a perfectly smooth spread. With random start positions, the paper notes that uneven clumps also cause early movement deep inside the crowd.
understand.quote: Figure 5 makes clear that opinion changes start at the extremes and are there (at the start!) most extreme for the most extreme opinions.

connect.caption: This is the paper's bounded-confidence rule (BC). Your next opinion x_{i}(t+1) is the plain average of everyone in I, the set of people whose opinions are within ε of yours. In the model, x_{i} is the slider for your opinion and ε is the listening-range slider. Because the model treats the crowd as a smooth even spread, the average of that set is just the midpoint of your window, cut off at 0 and 1. The curve plots that average minus x_{i}, which is the per-round change the paper calls Δ_{i}.

concepts.recap: Averaging moves you only when the people you hear are lopsided around you, so the first to move are the opinions at the edges, and they are pulled toward the centre.

concepts.title: Listening more to your own side
concepts.idea: If people further left or right tilt their listening window toward their own side, the inward pull at the edges weakens and can vanish, so the extremes stay put.

predict.question: New case: only people LEFT of centre lean toward their own side at full strength. People right of centre keep balanced windows. After the first round of averaging, which edge still moves toward the centre?
options: Only the top edge still moves inward
Only the bottom edge still moves inward
Both edges still move inward
Neither edge moves
why: Right. The top edge still has a balanced window, so it hears only people below it and is pulled down. The fully leaning bottom edge points its whole window off the scale and stays put.
This reverses the roles. The leaning side is the one whose window points off the scale, so the bottom edge loses its upward pull. The balanced top edge keeps its one-sided influence.
This would hold with no lean at all. A full lean removes the bottom edge's upward pull, so only the balanced top edge keeps moving inward.
A lean only switches off the pull where people lean. The top edge's window is still balanced, so it is still pulled down toward the people below it.

terms.means: A lean in the listening window that grows the further your opinion is from the centre: left-leaning people listen more to the left, right-leaning people more to the right
A listening window that reaches further on one side of your opinion than on the other

model.title: How far each opinion moves in the first round of averaging
model.note: Teaching model: opinions start as a smooth, perfectly even spread from 0 to 1, and only the first round is shown. With no lean, each person hears everyone within ε on both sides, so the window is 2ε wide. The lean keeps that width but shifts the window. The share pointing upward is (1 − m)/2 + m × opinion, as in the paper's Section 4.2.2. The paper's ε in that section is the total window width, so our ε is half of it. The paper ran full simulations. This curve is only a first-round sketch. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: Same picture as before: the solid curve shows how far each starting opinion moves in one round. A dashed copy now keeps the old version, so you can compare.
One new slider: how much people lean their listening window toward their own side of the scale. At 0 the window is balanced. At 1 the lean is as strong as it gets.
This box tracks the push on the person sitting at the very bottom. Keep an eye on it.

explore.prompt: Play with the lean and the listening range. Can you switch off the inward pull at the edges, even when people listen widely?

goals.text: Make the inward push on the person at the very bottom (almost) disappear
hints: The push at the edge comes from the part of the window that points toward the centre.
Which slider shrinks the part of an edge person's window that points inward?
Push the lean slider m all the way up.

goals.text: With a wide listening range (ε at least 0.4), put yourself at the very top and make your opinion stay put
hints: First set a wide listening range and move yourself to the top. Watch how hard you are pulled down.
At the top, a full lean points your whole window upward, where nobody is.
Widen ε, move yourself to the top, then raise the lean as far as it goes.

feedback.correct: Yes. A lean only removes the inward pull for people whose window actually tilts. A balanced edge still has one-sided influence and still moves toward the centre.
feedback.incorrect: The inward pull at an edge exists because the edge person hears only voices from the centre side. A full lean points their window off the scale, so that pull goes away. But this happens only where people lean. A balanced edge keeps being pulled inward.

steps.say: Start with no lean and put yourself at the very bottom. You hear only people above you, so averaging pushes you up by 0.075. That is the one-sided influence from before.

Now let people lean toward their own side. The further from the centre you are, the more of your window points outward. The paper calls this an opinion-dependent bias. At the centre the window stays balanced.

Your window now reaches further down than up. It is an asymmetric confidence interval. At the bottom edge, the downward part points at nobody. You listen upward only 0.075, so the push is halved to about 0.038.
Turn the lean all the way up. Your upward reach drops to zero, and the only opinion you hear is your own. The push is gone: the extreme stays where it is.
Check the centre. At 0.5 the window is still balanced, and the move is still zero. The lean changes the edges, not the middle.
Even wide listening doesn't help. Go to the top with ε = 0.4. Without a lean (dashed curve) you'd be pulled down by 0.2. With the full lean you don't move at all.

Compare the two curves. The dashed one has big inward pushes at both ends, which shrink the whole spread. The solid one is flat at the edges and even dips slightly outward. The squeeze toward the centre has disappeared.

understand.explanation: With a balanced window, people at the edges hear only voices from the centre side, so averaging pulls them inward and the whole spread shrinks. With an opinion-dependent bias, each person's window slides toward their own side. At an edge, the part pointing outward lands on empty space, and fewer centre voices are heard. As the lean grows, the inward pull at the edges weakens. At full lean it vanishes, and the extremes stay put. In Section 4.2.2 the paper simulated this with a regular start profile of 50 opinions and a total window of 0.6. Raising m past about 0.4 broke the consensus into two camps. At m = 0.99 the extremes did not move and slowly gathered nearby opinions. These are results from a simple model, not measurements of real people. Our curve shows only the first round of an even spread.
understand.quote: The principle cause for all these effects is that with an increasing m those at the extremes become less and less affected by opinions more in the centre of the opinion space.

connect.caption: This is the paper's rule from Section 4.2.2. β_r(x) is the share of the window pointing upward for someone at opinion x. m is the lean slider. ε_r and ε_l are your upward and downward reach in the model. The paper's ε_total is the full window width, which equals 2 × our ε slider. At m = 0 both sides get half. At m = 1 someone at 0 gets no upward reach at all.

concepts.recap: Tilt each listening window toward your own side, and the edges stop hearing the centre: their inward pull fades and, at full lean, the extremes stay where they are.

concepts.title: Why middling open-mindedness ends in two camps
concepts.idea: Edge opinions bunch up and pull in their neighbours, which opens a gap wider than ε in the middle. Once that split appears, the two sides never hear each other again, so two camps are locked in.

predict.question: A town with a middle listening range has ended up in two camps whose gap is wider than that range. Which change would let the camps finally reach each other?
options: Let them keep talking for many more rounds
Widen everyone's listening range so it is larger than the gap between the camps
Add more people to the bigger camp
Rerun the same crowd from the start with a narrower listening range
why: Tempting, because talk usually brings people closer. But across the gap nobody hears anybody, so extra rounds only tighten each camp on itself.
Correct: the camps stay apart only because the gap is wider than the range. Make the range larger than the gap and the two sides are heard again, so averaging can pull them together.
A bigger camp might seem to 'pull harder'. But people only average opinions they can hear, and nobody in the other camp can hear anyone across the gap, however many people sit there.
A narrower range seems to calm things down. In fact it makes gaps open more easily, which gives more surviving groups, not one.

terms.means: A gap between neighbouring opinions that is wider than the listening range ε, so people on either side no longer hear each other
The paper's name for the groups on either side of a split, which no longer influence each other

model.title: A crowd of 100 people settling their opinions
model.note: Teaching model: 100 people hold opinions from 0 to 1. Each round, everyone at once moves to the average of all opinions within the listening range: the paper's own rule. Groups are counted by gaps wider than 0.1, so tiny stray groups at the edges also count. Ranges below 0.06 are left out because nearby groups there would be merged in the count. The paper used 625 people, so its switch points differ a little. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data. The new slider stops the talk after a chosen number of rounds.

steps.say: This is the same crowd as before. Each dot is one person's opinion between 0 and 1, and each round everyone moves to the average of the opinions inside their listening range.
The random-crowd slider deals out a fresh set of starting opinions, and the boxes count the groups and how far apart the extremes end up.
New: this slider sets how long the crowd keeps talking. Short runs show the crowd part-way through. Long runs show where it settles.

explore.prompt: Pick a middle listening range, then play with the talking time and the starting crowd. Do the two camps ever find each other again?

goals.text: Choose a middle listening range (0.2 to 0.3) and let the crowd talk the full 20 rounds: end with two or more camps far apart (extremes more than 0.3 apart).
hints: At the default range everyone hears almost everyone. Which slider makes people less open-minded?
Bring the listening range down into the middle zone, and keep the talking time at its maximum.
Camps appear just below the range where the whole crowd still joins up. Narrow it a step at a time from 0.3.

goals.text: Keep a middle range and the full 20 rounds, but switch to a different random starting crowd. Get two or more far-apart camps again.
goals.when: seed >= 2 && conf >= 0.2 && conf <= 0.3 && rounds >= 20 && groups >= 2 && spread > 0.3
hints: One crowd could be a fluke. Which slider deals out a new crowd?
Move the random-crowd slider away from 1, and keep the range between 0.2 and 0.3.
Most crowds split at these ranges. If one joins up, deal another.

feedback.correct: Right. Once the gap is wider than the listening range, only a range wider than the gap lets the two sides hear each other again. Time, numbers and luck do not help.
feedback.incorrect: It is natural to think enough talk or enough people will bring the camps together. But in this model people only move toward opinions they can hear. Across a gap wider than the range, nobody hears anybody, so nothing can carry anyone across.

steps.say: Start where we left off: a wide listening range and a long talk. Everyone ends up in one group.

Now make people middlingly open-minded, a range of 0.24, and stop after a single round. Look at the two ends of the line: people there only hear voices on their inner side, so they have started moving inward and bunching up.
At round 2 the bunches near each end act like magnets. They pull in nearby people who can hear them. Those people leave the middle, so the middle thins out.
When the empty stretch between the two bunches grows wider than the listening range, nobody on one side can hear anybody on the other. The paper calls this a split.

After a split the two sides become separate opinion worlds. Each side only averages with itself. By round 6, when the paper's own example had split, the camps have only tightened. They do not move together.
Run to 20 rounds and nothing changes across the gap. The two camps stay apart. Extra time cannot repair a split.
Deal a different random crowd at the same range. The details shift, but the same thing happens: the edges bunch up, the middle empties, and two camps are left.

That is the surprise. People who listen to a fairly wide range of views, but not to everyone, usually do not meet in the middle. The edges bunch up and pull the centre apart, and two lasting camps lock in.

understand.explanation: People at the edges hear only voices on their inner side, so they drift inward and bunch up. These dense bunches then pull in the people within reach, which empties the middle. Once the empty gap is wider than the listening range, the two sides cannot hear each other, so no amount of further talk brings them together. The paper showed this by following an evenly spaced row of 50 opinions with a range of 0.2: the profile split after 6 rounds and stayed split. Across many random runs with 625 people, middle-sized ranges typically ended in two camps. These are idealised models, not observations of real societies, and the paper notes that restricting talk to local neighbours may make this polarisation disappear.
understand.quote: Under simultaneous updating cracked profiles can never get connected again. Agents/opinions outside ones own sub profile are ‘out of range/reach’ in a quite severe sense: They are not only outside ones own confidence interval, but also outside the confidence intervals of all others one takes seriously, outside the confidence intervals of all others which those others take seriously etc.

check.task: Show that the camps are settled early. Use a middle listening range (0.2 to 0.32), stop the talk at 6 rounds or fewer, and still end with two or more camps whose extremes are more than 0.3 apart.
check.hint: Set a middle range first, then pull the talking-time slider down to 6 or below.
check.misconception: That two camps are just a slow road to agreement, and that with enough time they would drift together. In fact the split is decided early, and later rounds only tighten each camp.

connect.caption: This is the paper's bounded-confidence rule (BC), which the model runs exactly. Each person's next opinion is the plain average of everyone within ε of them. ε is the listening range slider, and t counts the rounds set by the talking-time slider. A split is a gap with |x_{i} − x_{j}| > ε: across it, nobody is in anyone's set I, so the two sides never mix again.

concepts.recap: With middling open-mindedness, the edges bunch up and pull the middle apart. Once the gap is wider than the listening range, the two camps can never hear each other again.
